chapter: Idaho tours, Music Town and retirement
title: The Owens family and Biddy Mason's descendants
summary: Spikes knew Biddy Mason's descendants and tells how the Owens family came by ox cart from Texas, took her in, and later owned a block on Olive.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You said that Biddy Mason died in the 1890s...
So you missed knowing her but you said you her children and her family.

I knew her children and her grandchildren and her great grandchildren and her great grandchildren, and I knew her children. Yeah. And there's a building right there where that little house...home I showed you Third and ...mmm...Spring Street. There's a building there--a big building there--called the Owens Building. That was her...her...uh, grandson. Her daughter married...one of the girls who came here as a slave...married a fellow named Owens. He was a...he and his son came here in a oxcart from Texas, and he was half white, and his brother was a white man, and he owned a big grocery store in Oxnard, I think it was, and Owens and his son and daugh...moth...wife and two girls stopped in Los Angeles. They didn't go to Oxnard where his brother was, and they found a pla... uh, an old livery stable that was vacant at First and Los Angeles. I got a picture of that here somewhere, and they opened up the livery stable, and he used to buy horses. He got a contract with the Army, and he'd buy horses for the Army and send...and sometimes he'd go far as nearly to San Diego and pick up horses all along the way and come back for the Army and so...and get feed and everything for the

Army so he had a pretty nice thing going. And when Biddy was in court and they freed her, she didn't have no place to go, so he and the judge was friends so he took Biddy and her daughters in his home and kept them and...until they got work and things. And then his son married one of Biddy's daughters, and from that on, it was Bob Owens, and Bob Owens right now, where the Los Angeles Bicentennial Committee's headquarters is, is, I think it's 16 or 17 or 18 North... North...uh, South Olive Street--this Owens used to own that whole block from Sixth to Seventh on Olive, and he was a colored man but he came here from Texas in the oxcart, and after a few years and everything, he went up to visit his brother in Oxnard, then he died up there. And that's the story. I got all of it here, and...
You've done a lot of research!
No, Marilyn [Miriam Matthews ] give me all that. She had it all researched, and she gave me all of that stuff. But I've got the whole history of it here, and he died up there. Cut it off a minute.
